readerTitle: Why half your new customers quit on page three
caseNote: 가상 사례 (팔레트 화물 운송사의 신규 거래처 신청서, 가계부 앱 가입 화면) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 가입 이탈은 고객의 의지 문제가 아니라, 지금 꼭 필요하지 않은 요구와 잘못 놓인 기본값이 만든 설계 문제다.
misconception: 가입을 끝까지 안 하는 사람은 원래 관심이 없던 사람이다. 혜택을 더 얹으면 해결된다.

sources.text: 행동경제학의 표준 개념 (마찰, 기본값 효과). 이 유닛의 개념 레슨 CUS-05-02, CUS-05-03 참고
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 3번 카드의 단계별 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 계산 확인: 200명 시작 → 회사 정보 150명 → 신용·보험 서류 60명 → 완료 50명. 완료율 50 ÷ 200 = 25%. 가장 큰 이탈은 150 → 60 (90명, 회사 정보 단계 통과자의 60%).
7번 카드에서 사전 체크된 유료 옵션이 일부 지역에서 규제될 수 있다는 점은 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않도록 '신뢰를 잃는다'는 일반적인 표현으로만 적었습니다. 특정 국가 규정은 언급하지 않습니다.

cards.title: Why half your new customers quit on page three
body: A regional pallet-shipping company gets plenty of interest. Small manufacturers fill in its online account form to book their first freight run.
Then most of them vanish. Not on page one. On page three, the one asking for credit references and an insurance certificate.

image.label: A long paper form trailing off a desk, with a pallet truck waiting outside
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 창고 사무실 책상 위에 바닥까지 늘어지는 긴 신청서. 창밖에는 팔레트를 실은 트럭이 출발을 기다림. 실제 회사 로고와 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run the shipping company. What do you change first?
body: Your form has four pages: contact details, company details, credit and insurance documents, then shipping preferences. Only one in four people who start it finish.
Which fix would you try first?

options.text: Ask only what you need to quote and book a first shipment. Collect the rest later
options.feedback: This removes **friction** where people stall. You give up some paperwork upfront, but you get far more customers through the door.

options.text: Offer 10% off the first shipment for finishing the form
options.feedback: More motivation can help, but the hard page is still there. You pay the discount to everyone, including people who would have finished anyway.

options.text: Have sales call everyone who drops off
options.feedback: You'll rescue some accounts and learn why people quit. But it's costly, and it treats the symptom instead of the form.

cards.title: One page did most of the damage.
body: Most people weren't unwilling. They were asked for documents they didn't have at hand, for a decision they hadn't made yet. They meant to come back. Few did.
cards.softwareNote: Most sign-up tools can show this step-by-step funnel. Look for the single steepest drop before rewriting the whole flow.

cards.title: Ask for things when they're needed.
body: **Friction** is every bit of effort between a customer and what they want: a field, a document, a decision. People weigh it against how badly they want the thing *right now*.
A first-time shipper wants a quote and a pickup date. Credit references only matter if they ask for 30-day payment terms. So move that request to the moment someone actually asks for credit.
The paperwork doesn't disappear. It just stops blocking the first sale.

cards.title: How should new customers pay?
body: The form now offers two options: *pay per shipment by card* or *open a credit account with 30-day terms*. Credit accounts need the document checks.
What should be selected when the page opens?

options.text: Pay by card, with credit terms offered after a few shipments
options.feedback: The **default** puts most people on the easy path, and it fits a brand-new customer. You lose some early credit accounts, but they can still choose it.

options.text: Credit account, since bigger customers prefer it
options.feedback: The **default** would send everyone back into the document page that caused the drop-off. The few who want credit can pick it themselves.
Neutral and fair, but it adds a decision at a fragile moment. Some people will stop to think about terms they don't care about yet.

cards.title: The pre-selected option is a decision you make for them.
body: Most people keep whatever is already filled in. That makes a **default** powerful: it decides which path most customers walk, and how much friction they meet along the way.
A good default matches what most customers would choose if they thought about it. Here, new shippers testing a carrier would rarely want to fill in a credit application first.

image.label: Two paths from a form: a short smooth road selected, a longer road with paperwork
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 신청서에서 갈라지는 두 길. 체크 표시된 짧고 평탄한 길 "Pay by card", 서류 더미가 놓인 긴 길 "Credit account". 대부분의 작은 인물들이 체크된 길로 걸어감.

cards.title: Not all friction is bad. Not all defaults are fair.
body: Some friction protects you. Credit checks stop unpaid invoices. Fraud checks stop bad accounts. Remove those and sign-ups rise while losses rise too, so track how many new accounts actually ship and pay, not just how many finish the form.
Defaults can also be abused. A pre-ticked paid add-on may lift revenue for a month, then break trust when customers notice. Set defaults you'd be happy to explain out loud.

cards.title: Now it's a budgeting app.
body: Before seeing anything, new users must enter email, password and phone code, link a bank account, and pick one of four plans. Many quit at the bank link.

options.text: Let people explore with sample data first, default to the free plan, ask for the bank link later
options.feedback: This cuts **friction** before users see the value, and the **default** fits a cautious first visit. You'll see fewer bank links on day one, but from people who've decided they want them.

options.text: Drop the phone code and keep everything else
options.feedback: One less step helps a little. But the big obstacle, handing over bank access to an app they haven't tried, is still in the way.

options.text: Pre-select the annual premium plan with a free trial that auto-renews
options.feedback: The **default** works against the customer. Paid sign-ups may jump, then refunds, complaints and quiet cancellations follow.

cards.title: Sign-up drop-off is usually a design problem.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Friction** (CUS-05-02): ask only for what you need now, and move the rest to when it matters. **Defaults** (CUS-05-03): pre-select the path most customers would choose for themselves.
**Try it today:** go through your own sign-up as a new customer. Mark every field *needed now*, *needed later* or *never needed*.
